findings.claim: The question is exact-only (ex:1), so plainly right answers such as "under 22", "below 22" and "less than 22" are marked wrong. The list accepts "22" on its own and "under 22 percent", but not these bare forms.
findings.because: In matchSA (C:/Users/zpull/SommeliersCodex/js/core.js), q.ex stops grading after the exact normalized comparison, so no containment or number-token matching runs. None of the accept entries equals norm("under 22"), norm("below 22") or norm("less than 22"). The keyed fact itself is correct: Liquor Tax Act Art. 3(7) defines seishu as a strained rice brew under 22 degrees alcohol.

findings.verifyReason: The finding holds. The live entry in js/data-questions.js is the same as the batch copy: ex:1, and the accept list has "22", "22 degrees", "under 22 percent" and "under 22%", but no bare "under/below/less than 22" forms. I loaded the actual matchSA and norm from core.js into node and ran it on this question. "22", "22 percent", "under 22%" and "twenty-two percent" grade true. "under 22", "below 22", "less than 22" and "under twenty two" all grade false. That is because the q.ex branch skips the numeric-token and containment checks, and norm("under 22") matches no accept entry exactly. "under 22 degrees" also grades false, even though "22 degrees" is accepted, which is the same flaw with the unit the Act itself uses (二十二度未満). The keyed fact is not disputed: Liquor Tax Act Art. 3(7) puts seishu under 22 degrees alcohol. The examiner's fix is right but misses the degree forms, so the better fix adds those too.

question.q: Japan's Liquor Tax Act refuses the name seishu to any rice brew at or above a certain strength. Where does that ceiling sit?
question.exp: The same definition demands that the fermenting mash be strained, which is why doburoku, the unstrained farm brew, is legally not sake at all, and why even the murkiest nigori has passed through at least a coarse mesh. The ceiling is also the outer legal wall for undiluted genshu: a rice brew at twenty-two or above changes legal identity, though in practice the yeast gives out first and most genshu land between seventeen and twenty percent.
